Absentee Shawnee

The Absentee Shawnee Tribe of Indians of Oklahoma is a distinct Shawnee tribal government based in the Shawnee area. Its histories connect Ohio Valley homelands, displacement through several regions, and community life in Oklahoma. Tribal sources foreground the Big Jim and White Turkey communities and the continuing importance of language and cultural preservation.

Names & relationshipsAbsentee Shawnee, Eastern Shawnee, and the Shawnee Tribe are three distinct tribal governments. Shared Shawnee histories and language do not make them interchangeable.
An expanded introduction, with sources reviewed.This profile develops several themes through identified sources. Citations connect each section to its evidence; remaining gaps appear below. It has not been reviewed or endorsed by the community.
01

Shawnee relationships and political identity

The Eastern Shawnee Tribe’s own history identifies three federally recognized Shawnee governments in Oklahoma: Eastern Shawnee, Absentee Shawnee, and the Shawnee Tribe. That distinction matters when using sources: an account of one government’s treaty history, programs, or citizenship should not automatically be assigned to another. The Absentee Shawnee government and health system publish their own accounts, providing the most direct starting points for this particular community.

Read the sources [3] Eastern Shawnee Tribe of Oklahoma [2] Absentee Shawnee Tribe of Indians of Oklahoma

02

Dispersal and the Absentee name

The tribe’s health-system history places ancestral Shawnee homelands in the Ohio Valley. During and after the American Revolution, displacement carried communities into Missouri and subsequently farther south and west. The Absentee name refers to Shawnee people living away from the Kansas reservation associated with nineteenth-century U.S. arrangements. This was a history of repeated movement under colonial pressure.

Read the sources [1] Absentee Shawnee Tribal Health System

03

Communities and land in Oklahoma

The tribal account describes settlement around the Canadian River and land title in 1872. It discusses the Big Jim and White Turkey communities and differences in their responses to assimilation pressures. Allotment in the 1890s transformed landholding again. These names help explain internal history without making every band a separate modern government.

Read the sources [1] Absentee Shawnee Tribal Health System

04

Government and public institutions

The tribal health system describes a constitutional government organized under the Oklahoma Indian Welfare Act, with an elected five-member Executive Committee. The government’s public website gives direct access to its institutions and publications. These sources also document continuing responsibilities for services and community life, beyond the historical summary of displacement and settlement.

Read the sources [1] Absentee Shawnee Tribal Health System [2] Absentee Shawnee Tribe of Indians of Oklahoma

05

Language and cultural preservation

The tribe’s January 2026 newspaper describes an Among the Shawnee podcast episode involving language and historic-preservation staff, discussing community history and language preservation. A separate Shawnee Tribe article from 2024 reports a language cohort involving Absentee Shawnee elder George Fife Blanchard. These are distinct publishers and initiatives. Together they document both community-specific work and relationships across Shawnee governments, without supplying a reliable current total of speakers or a complete account of language teaching.

Read the sources [4] Absentee Shawnee Tribe of Indians of Oklahoma [5] Shawnee Tribe

What needs further research

  • Add direct treaty text and more community-authored land and allotment histories.
  • Expand coverage of tribal education, arts, and community perspectives beyond institutional summaries.
